title: f-strings

items.title: What Are f-Strings?
items.content: f-strings (formatted string literals) were introduced in Python 3.6 as a modern, readable way to embed expressions inside string literals. They are prefixed with an f or F and use curly braces {} to evaluate variables or expressions at runtime. Unlike older methods such as % formatting or str.format(), f-strings are concise and evaluated immediately. Example: name = 'Ada'; age = 12; print(f'Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.') This outputs: Hello, Ada! You are 12 years old. F-strings are especially useful when displaying user input because they keep the code clean and easy to read.
items.explanation: Strings in Python are immutable sequences of Unicode characters enclosed in single, double, or triple quotes. Because strings cannot be modified in place, all transformations return new string instances.

items.prompt: Which of the following is the correct way to create an f-string in Python?
items.explanation: An f-string must start with the letter f (or F) before the opening quote. Expressions inside the string are placed in curly braces {}. The other options either use concatenation, omit the f prefix, or use incorrect syntax.

items.title: f-String Syntax Rules
items.content: The basic syntax of an f-string is: f'text {expression} more text'. The expression inside { } can be a variable, a literal, a function call, or even a mathematical operation. Important rules: (1) The f prefix must appear immediately before the opening quote. (2) Curly braces { } are evaluated at runtime. (3) You cannot use single quotes inside an f-string delimited by single quotes without escaping, unless you use double quotes. Example: score = 85; print(f"Your score is {score}.") This prints Your score is 85.. Understanding this syntax is essential before combining f-strings with user input.

items.prompt:
Given the code below, what will be printed?

name = 'Sam'
print(f'Hi {name}')
items.explanation: The variable name is evaluated inside the curly braces and replaced with its value 'Sam'. Therefore, the output is Hi Sam. The braces are not printed literally because this is a valid f-string.

items.prompt:
Which output correctly matches the f-string code?

city = 'Paris'
print(f'I live in {city}.')
items.explanation: The variable city is substituted with its value 'Paris' inside the f-string. The period is part of the literal text, so the complete output is I live in Paris..

items.prompt: Which of the following is a common pitfall when using f-strings with user input?
options: User input is automatically converted to uppercase
Missing the f prefix causes the variable to be printed literally
f-strings only work with strings, not integers
items.correct_answer: Missing the f prefix causes the variable to be printed literally
items.explanation: If you forget the f prefix, Python treats the braces as a literal set of characters and does not evaluate the variable. For example, print('Hello {name}') prints Hello {name} instead of substituting the value. F-strings handle both strings and integers automatically.

items.prompt:
What is the output of the following code?

user_input = '42'
print(f'You entered: {user_input}')
items.explanation: The f-string evaluates user_input and inserts its value '42' into the string. No newline is added unless explicitly written as \n in the literal.

items.prompt:
Predict the exact output of this program:

age = 15
print(f'Age: {age}')
print(f'Age squared: {age * age}')
items.explanation: The first f-string prints Age: 15. The second evaluates age * age, which is 15 * 15 = 225, and prints Age squared: 225. print() adds a newline after each statement, so the output appears on two lines without an extra trailing newline in the string itself.

items.prompt:
What will this code display?

name = input('Enter your name: ')
print(f'Welcome, {name}!')
options: Error: input not allowed in f-strings
items.explanation: input() pauses execution and waits for the user to type a value. If the user types Alice and presses Enter, name becomes 'Alice'. The f-string then prints Welcome, Alice!. The prompt text appears before the input cursor.

items.prompt:
Analyze the following code and identify the issue:

score = 100
print(f'Score: {score + 10}')
options: The code is valid and prints Score: 110
The code raises a TypeError because score is not a string
The code requires parentheses around the expression
items.correct_answer: The code is valid and prints Score: 110
items.explanation: F-strings evaluate any valid Python expression inside { }. score + 10 computes 110, so the output is Score: 110. There is no error and no need for extra parentheses.

items.prompt:
Trace the execution and determine the final output:

first = 'Jane'
last = 'Doe'
full = f'{first} {last}'
print(full.upper())
items.explanation: The f-string creates 'Jane Doe'. Calling .upper() on that string returns 'JANE DOE'. print() displays it without quotes. The output is JANE DOE on one line.

items.prompt:
What is the output of this script?

items = 3
print(f'Items: {items}')
print(f'Items: {items + 1}')
print(f'Items: {items * 2}')
items.explanation: The first f-string prints the variable items (3). The second evaluates items + 1 (4). The third evaluates items * 2 (6). Each print statement outputs its own line.

items.prompt: Complete the f-string: f'Hello, ___!'
items.explanation: To embed a variable named name inside an f-string, you must use curly braces {name}. Without braces, the text is literal. Double braces {{ and }} would escape the braces and print them as characters.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank: The f-string prefix must be written as ___ before the opening quote.
items.explanation: The f-string literal must begin with the lowercase letter f (or uppercase F) immediately preceding the quote. This tells Python to evaluate expressions inside curly braces at runtime.

items.prompt: Reorder the following code lines to correctly ask for a user's age and print it using an f-string.
items.explanation: First, collect input with input(). Then convert it to an integer with int() so it can be used in calculations if needed. Finally, display the result with an f-string. print('How old are you? ') alone is not sufficient because it does not capture the user's response.

items.prompt: Complete the f-string to display the user's name and age: `f'Hello, my name is ___ and I am ___ years old.'`
items.explanation: In an f-string, variables are embedded using curly braces {}. The expressions inside the braces are evaluated and their values are inserted directly into the string. Here, {name} and {age} are placeholders that will be replaced by the actual variable values when the f-string is evaluated.

items.prompt: Arrange the following code lines in the correct order to create an f-string that greets the user by name:
items.explanation: The correct sequence is: first, prompt the user for input and store it in the variable name; second, use an f-string with {name} to interpolate the variable into the greeting. The f-string must come after the variable is defined, otherwise it will raise a NameError.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank to compute the area of a rectangle using an f-string: `print(f'Area: {length * width}')` uses multiplication. To format to 2 decimal places, use: `print(f'Area: {length * width:___}')`
items.explanation: The format specifier .2f inside an f-string formats a number as a fixed-point decimal with exactly 2 digits after the decimal point. This is a common idiom for displaying floating-point calculations cleanly.

items.prompt: Identify the error in this code snippet that attempts to use an f-string.
items.starter_code:
x = 10
y = 20
print(f'The sum is {x + y')
items.solution_code:
x = 10
y = 20
print(f'The sum is {x + y}')
items.hint: Check the closing quote and the placement of the expression inside the f-string.
items.explanation: The error is a missing closing single quote after the expression inside the f-string. The correct syntax requires the expression to be enclosed in curly braces and the entire f-string to be closed with a matching quote. The corrected line is: print(f'The sum is {x + y}').

name = 'Alice'
print('Welcome to the class, ' + name + '!')
items.hint: Replace the string concatenation with an f-string that embeds the variable name.
items.explanation: The original code uses string concatenation with the + operator, which is less readable and error-prone. The fix replaces it with an f-string: f'Welcome to the class, {name}!', which directly interpolates the variable name into the string.

items.prompt: Fix the code to safely display a user's balance, which may be a float, and handle the case where the balance is zero.
items.hint: Ensure the f-string handles the float value correctly and formats it to two decimal places.
items.explanation: The original code works but does not format the float. The fixed code uses the format specifier .2f to ensure consistent decimal display, and the conditional logic ensures the message remains clear even when the balance is zero.

items.prompt: Diagnose the runtime error in this program that reads a score and displays it.
items.starter_code:
score = int(input('Enter your score: '))
print(f'Your score is {score_}')
items.solution_code:
score = int(input('Enter your score: '))
print(f'Your score is {score}')
items.hint: Compare the variable name used in the input with the variable name used in the f-string.
items.explanation: A NameError occurs at runtime because the f-string references score_ (with an underscore), which was never defined. The variable defined by input is score (without underscore). The fix is to use {score} in the f-string.

items.prompt: Repair the logic so the f-string correctly reports whether a number is even or odd.
items.hint: The code structure is correct; verify the modulo operation and f-string placement.
items.explanation: The starter code is actually correct as written. The modulo operator % checks for evenness, and the f-strings correctly embed the number. No changes were needed. This item tests careful reading: sometimes the code works and the 'fix' is to confirm correctness.

items.prompt: Refactor this inefficient string-building code into a single optimized f-string.
items.starter_code:
first = 'John'
last = 'Doe'
age = 30
middle = ' '
result = 'Name: ' + first + middle + last + ', Age: ' + str(age) + '
items.solution_code:
first = 'John'
last = 'Doe'
age = 30
result = f'Name: {first} {last}, Age: {age}\n'
items.hint: Use one f-string to combine all variables and avoid explicit concatenation.
items.explanation: The original code uses multiple + operations and an unnecessary middle variable. The refactored version uses a single f-string with {first}, {last}, and {age}, eliminating intermediate variables and improving readability and performance.

items.prompt: Write a program that reads a price and quantity, calculates the total, and displays it formatted to 2 decimal places using an f-string.
items.starter_code:
# TODO: Implement solution for f-strings
# Follow requirements outlined in the prompt
items.solution_code:

quantity = int(input('Enter the quantity: '))
total = price * quantity
print(f'Total cost: ${total:.2f}')
items.hint: Convert inputs to the correct numeric types, compute the total, and use .2f in the f-string.
items.explanation: This practical example shows f-strings with arithmetic expressions ({price * quantity}) and format specifiers (.2f) to ensure monetary values display consistently with two decimal places.

items.prompt: Write a program that reads a birth year, computes age (assuming current year is 2024), and prints a personalized message. If age is under 18, add 'You are a minor.'; otherwise, add 'You are an adult.' Use a conditional expression inside the f-string.
items.starter_code:
# TODO: Implement solution for f-strings
# Follow requirements outlined in the prompt
items.solution_code:
birth_year = int(input('Enter your birth year: '))
age = 2024 - birth_year
status = 'You are a minor.' if age < 18 else 'You are an adult.'
print(f'Born in {birth_year}, you are {age} years old. {status}')

test_cases.expected: Born in 2010, you are 14 years old. You are a minor.
Born in 1990, you are 34 years old. You are an adult.

items.hint: Use a ternary conditional expression inside the f-string to choose the status message.
items.explanation: This advanced example combines arithmetic, conditional expressions (if-else inline), and multiple f-string interpolations. The ternary operator is evaluated at runtime and its result is embedded directly in the output string.

items.prompt: Real-world scenario: Build a simple order summary. Read the item name, unit price, and quantity. Compute the subtotal and, if quantity > 5, apply a 10% discount. Display the final amount formatted as currency using an f-string. Validate that inputs are positive numbers.
items.starter_code:
# TODO: Implement solution for f-strings
# Follow requirements outlined in the prompt
items.solution_code:
item = input('Item name: ')
price = float(input('Unit price: '))
quantity = int(input('Quantity: '))
if price <= 0 or quantity <= 0:
    print('Invalid input: price and quantity must be positive.')
else:
    subtotal = price * quantity
    if quantity > 5:
        discount = subtotal * 0.10
        total = subtotal - discount
        print(f'{item}: ${subtotal:.2f} with 10% discount applied. Final: ${total:.2f}')
    else:
        total = subtotal
        print(f'{item}: ${subtotal:.2f}. Final: ${total:.2f}')
items.hint: Calculate subtotal, apply conditional discount logic, and format all monetary values with .2f in f-strings.
items.explanation: This synthesis task integrates input validation, arithmetic, conditional logic, and formatted output. f-strings are used to present a clean, readable order summary with currency formatting.

items.prompt: Mastery challenge: Write a program that reads a full name and a birth date (YYYY-MM-DD), parses the date, computes age, and prints a certificate-style message. Use an f-string with a date formatting specifier (strftime) to display the birth date as 'Month Day, Year'.
items.starter_code:
# TODO: Implement solution for f-strings
# Follow requirements outlined in the prompt
items.solution_code:
import datetime
full_name = input('Enter your full name: ')
birth_str = input('Enter birth date (YYYY-MM-DD): ')
birth_date = datetime.datetime.strptime(birth_str, '%Y-%m-%d')
current_year = datetime.datetime.now().year
age = current_year - birth_date.year - ((datetime.datetime.now().month, datetime.datetime.now().day) < (birth_date.month, birth_date.day))
birth_formatted = birth_date.strftime('%B %d, %Y')
print(f'CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION\n')
print(f'This certifies that {full_name} was born on {birth_formatted} and is {age} years old as of {datetime.datetime.now().year}.\n')
print(f'Congratulations, {full_name}!')

test_cases.expected: CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION\nThis certifies that Jane Doe was born on July 15, 1995 and is 29 years old as of 2024.\nCongratulations, Jane Doe!
CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION\nThis certifies that Sam Lee was born on January 01, 2000 and is 24 years old as of 2024.\nCongratulations, Sam Lee!

items.hint: Use datetime.strptime to parse the input, strftime to format the date, and compute age carefully accounting for whether the birthday has passed this year.
items.explanation: This mastery challenge requires datetime manipulation, precise age calculation, and complex f-string formatting with newlines and multiple interpolations. It demonstrates professional-level use of f-strings for structured, readable output.
